title: Oakhaven Welcomes Two New Leaders to its Executive Team
excerpt: Daniel Osei joins as Chief Operating Officer and Claire Brennan as Chief People Officer, as the portfolio passes one thousand employees.
imageAlt: Restored brick buildings along a downtown street

blocks.text: Oakhaven Holdings today announced two appointments to its executive team. Daniel Osei will serve as Chief Operating Officer, and Claire Brennan has been named Chief People Officer.

Osei brings 24 years of plant and supply chain leadership, most recently as vice president of operations at a Midwest maker of agricultural equipment. Brennan has led people teams at manufacturers and service businesses for 18 years, and grew up in the Alder Valley.
“We have grown to more than a thousand people across 24 companies. Daniel and Claire will help every one of those companies run well and look after the people in them.”
blocks.author: Margaret Whitford

blocks.text: Two new roles

Both positions are new. The Chief Operating Officer will work alongside portfolio company leaders on operations, purchasing and safety. The Chief People Officer will lead talent, benefits and Oakhaven’s Member Opportunities programmes.
Both start on September 1 and will be based at the Hartwell Building in Alder Falls.

title: The Long View, Episode 12: What a Seller Really Wants
excerpt: Three owners who sold their companies to Oakhaven talk about price, people and what made them say yes.
imageAlt: Restored brick buildings along a downtown street

blocks.text: In this episode, host Tomi Adeyemi sits down with three founders who sold their businesses to Oakhaven between 2015 and 2023.
They talk about the offers they turned down, the questions they asked us, and why the promise to keep the name on the door mattered more than the last dollar.
In this episode
Why price was the third question, not the first
What happened to the staff in the first year
The advice they would give an owner thinking of selling
“I wanted to know who would own my company in twenty years. Oakhaven was the only buyer who could answer that.”
blocks.author: Founder of Hollis Precision

title: Rail Spur Opens at Alder Junction, Readying 60 Acres for New Industry
excerpt: A new short-line connection makes Alder Junction one of the few rail-served industrial sites in the region with land ready to build on.
imageAlt: A freight train running past an industrial site

blocks.text: The first train ran on the new spur at Alder Junction this week, connecting Oakhaven’s 160-acre industrial campus to the regional short-line railroad.
The two-mile spur was built with a state economic development grant and Oakhaven’s own capital. It opens 60 undeveloped acres to manufacturers and distributors that ship by rail.
“Land with rail, power and water already in place is rare. We built the spur because the next generation of tenants will need it.”
blocks.author: James Thornton

blocks.text: Kestrel Logistics and Northbound Freight, both Oakhaven companies, already operate on the site. Cedar Row Properties will market the new parcels from this autumn.

title: Community Impact Report 2026: $312 Million in Economic Impact
excerpt: Oakhaven’s yearly report to the Trust’s members shows record revenue, a fourteenth consecutive distribution and more than a thousand jobs.
imageAlt: A city skyline lit up at night above a river

blocks.text: Oakhaven today published its Community Impact Report for fiscal 2025, presented to members of the Alder Valley Community Trust at their annual meeting.
Headline figures
$312 million in total economic impact, including direct, indirect and induced effects
$268 million in combined revenue across 24 companies
1,042 people employed directly
$9.6 million distributed to the Trust, the fourteenth year in a row
“These numbers belong to the members. Our job is to make sure they are bigger for the next generation than they are for this one.”
blocks.author: Erik Lindqvist

blocks.text: The report also sets out what did not go to plan, including a slower year for the advisory business, and what we are doing about it.

title: Oakhaven Federal Services Wins Five-Year Facilities Contract at a National Research Campus
excerpt: The award covers operations and maintenance across 40 buildings and is the largest in the Federal Group’s history.

blocks.text: Oakhaven Federal Services has been awarded a five-year contract for facilities operations and maintenance at a national research campus in the Pacific Northwest.

The team of 85 will look after 40 laboratory and office buildings, including power, heating and cooling, grounds and minor construction. Most of the current workforce will transfer to the new contract.
“The people who know a site are its greatest asset. Keeping them, and looking after them, is how we will earn the next five years.”
blocks.author: Daniel Osei

blocks.text: The award is the largest in the Federal Group’s history and its fourth at a research campus.

title: The Long View, Episode 11: Why Our Owners Can Wait
excerpt: Board chair Thomas Hale on patient capital, the 1997 vote and what a community endowment can do that a fund cannot.
imageAlt: Autumn sun over a quiet river valley

blocks.text: Thomas Hale has farmed in the Alder Valley all his life and has chaired Oakhaven’s board since the day it was formed. He joins Tomi Adeyemi to talk about what it means to invest without a deadline.
In this episode
The night the cooperative voted to sell, and why the money was never divided
How the board decides what the Trust can afford to wait for
The difference between patience and doing nothing
“My great-uncle planted an orchard he never saw bear fruit. That is the job.”
blocks.author: Thomas Hale

title: Brightline Circuits Opens a Second Plant, Keeping 120 Jobs in the Region
excerpt: Brightline Circuits has bought a neighbouring plant whose owner was retiring, keeping its 120 employees and adding capacity for medical customers.
imageAlt: Aerial view of a modern manufacturing plant

blocks.text: Brightline Circuits, an Oakhaven company, has bought a circuit board assembly plant 12 miles from its home at Millrace Works. The plant’s founder was retiring with no family successor.
All 120 employees have been offered roles with Brightline. The second plant adds clean-room space for medical device customers and doubles the company’s capacity for box builds.
“The people in that building had spent decades learning their trade. Losing that would have been a loss for the whole region.”
blocks.author: Margaret Whitford

title: Oakhaven Becomes a Limited Partner in Riverstone Capital
excerpt: A commitment to an early-stage fund backing founders in the Great Lakes states, Oakhaven’s second minority investment.

blocks.text: Oakhaven has committed capital to Riverstone Capital’s second fund as a limited partner. The fund invests in early-stage companies founded in the Great Lakes states.

The commitment is a small part of the portfolio by design. It gives Oakhaven a window onto the companies that may become tomorrow’s acquisition candidates, and supports founders who want to build close to home.
“We will never be venture investors. But we want the next generation of good companies to start here, and to stay here.”
blocks.author: James Thornton

title: The Long View, Episode 10: Inside the Hartwell Restoration
excerpt: The builder, the architect and the barn: how a vacant landmark became our home.
imageAlt: A black and white photograph of a brick building on a street corner

blocks.text: Ten years after work began on the Hartwell Building, the builder and architect who led the restoration walk Tomi Adeyemi through the building, floor by floor.
In this episode
What they found behind the plaster on the fourth floor
Taking down a cooperative barn, board by board
Why keeping the old stair cost more, and was worth it

title: Hollis Precision Named Manufacturer of the Year by the Regional Chamber
excerpt: The award recognises the company’s apprenticeship programme, which has trained 46 machinists since 2017.
imageAlt: A machinist at work on a lathe

blocks.text: Hollis Precision has been named Manufacturer of the Year by the regional chamber of commerce, in recognition of its growth and its apprenticeship programme.
Since 2017 the programme has trained 46 machinists, most of them from high schools within 30 miles of the plant. Thirty-nine still work at Hollis.
“Every machine we buy is only as good as the person running it. The apprentices are the best investment we have made.”
blocks.author: Plant manager

title: Kestrel Logistics and Northbound Freight Combine Operations at Alder Junction
excerpt: A shared cross-dock and dispatch centre will cut empty miles and give customers one point of contact for storage and freight.
imageAlt: Aerial view of an industrial park with warehouses

blocks.text: Kestrel Logistics and Northbound Freight, both Oakhaven companies, will share a new cross-dock and dispatch centre at Alder Junction from this autumn.
Customers will be able to store, pick and ship through a single contact, and the two companies expect to cut empty truck miles by around 15 percent.
Both companies keep their own names, leaders and teams.

title: Founders Tower Fully Leased for the First Time Since 2008
excerpt: Six years after a joint purchase and a floor-by-floor renovation, every office in the downtown landmark is let.
imageAlt: Downtown towers at dusk above the river

blocks.text: Founders Tower, the 18-storey landmark Oakhaven owns jointly with a partner foundation, is fully leased for the first time since 2008.
Since the purchase in 2019, Cedar Row Properties has renovated twelve floors, rebuilt the lobby and opened the top floor as an event space.
“A full building downtown is good for every business on the street. That was always part of the point.”
blocks.author: Erik Lindqvist
